pages.text: Before dawn, Lante woke to the smell of woodsmoke. It was Homowo day in Jamestown. His grandmother, Grandma Ablade, was already at work. “Come and see,” she said. “Today we hoot at hunger. But first, you must know why.”

It was Homowo day in Jamestown.
His grandmother, Grandma Ablade, was already at work.
“Come and see,” she said.
“Today we hoot at hunger.
But first, you must know why.”
pages.alt: A boy wakes to the smell of smoke while his grandmother works in the early morning light.

pages.text: “The word Homowo comes from two Ga words,” said Grandma Ablade. “Homo means hunger, and wo means to hoot or jeer. So it means hooting at hunger. We laugh at hunger because we are not afraid of it any more.” Naadu giggled and hooted, and Grandma hooted back.
sentences: “The word Homowo comes from two Ga words,” said Grandma Ablade.

So it means hooting at hunger.
We laugh at hunger because we are not afraid of it any more.” Naadu giggled and hooted, and Grandma hooted back.
pages.alt: A grandmother and her granddaughter laugh and hoot together in a kitchen yard.

pages.text: “Here is the story,” said Grandma. “Long ago, when the Ga people were on their long journey, a time of hunger came, and many people suffered. They prayed and poured libation and asked the ancestors and the gods for help. In time, good harvests came back. So every year we remember the hunger and give thanks for the food.” She added, “Some say it happened during the journey, and some say in the early days here. The tellers do not all agree.”

They prayed and poured libation and asked the ancestors and the gods for help.
In time, good harvests came back.
So every year we remember the hunger and give thanks for the food.” She added, “Some say it happened during the journey, and some say in the early days here.
The tellers do not all agree.”
pages.alt: People pray with a bowl of water beside a field of ripening grain.

pages.text: “Before the festival there is a time of quiet,” said Grandma. “For about four weeks, the noise ban is kept while the first grain is sown. People do not play loud drums or music in the streets. It is a way to show respect while the crops are planted.” Lante put a finger to his lips. “So the hooting comes after the hush.”

“So the hooting comes after the hush.”
pages.alt: A quiet street with a farmer sowing grain at the edge of town and no musicians.

pages.text: Grandma showed them the bowl. “This is kpokpoi,” she said. “We steam dough made from ground grain and knead it in a wooden bowl. Some tell it with millet and some with corn. Then we stir in palm oil and serve it with okra soup and fish. Today we cooked from about four o’clock, so that it would be ready by seven.”

pages.text: Then Grandma took a little kpokpoi in her hand. “First we sprinkle some on the ground,” she said. “That is for the ancestors. We say thank you for their care, and we ask them to stay close to us.” She scattered it gently and poured a little drink. Lante and Naadu watched silently, learning how to be respectful.

pages.alt: A grandmother gently sprinkles food on the ground while the children watch.

pages.text: “The Friday before, we celebrate the twins,” said Grandma. “Twins wear white and eat yam in the Twins Yam Festival. And on Saturday, everyone shares food with their neighbours. Relatives from other towns come home too. Many Ga people living far away hold Homowo as well, so the hooting goes round the world.”

And on Saturday, everyone shares food with their neighbours.
Relatives from other towns come home too.
Many Ga people living far away hold Homowo as well, so the hooting goes round the world.”
pages.alt: Twins in white eat from a shared dish while neighbours bring bowls of food.

pages.text: “And when is Homowo?” asked Naadu. “It is not on a fixed day,” said Grandma. “The Ga calendar is set by the priests and elders, so the date can shift by a week or two. It is usually in August, but sometimes in July or September.” Lante laughed. “So we hoot when the elders say!” “Exactly,” said Grandma, and passed him a big bowl. The end.

activities.prompt: Grandma says there is a time of quiet before the festival. Why might people keep quiet while the first grain is sown?
options: It is a way of showing respect for the crops and the season

activities.question: What do the Ga sprinkle on the ground first?
options: A little kpokpoi, for the ancestors

activities.definition: A drink poured out as a prayer or offering.

activities.prompt: Put the Homowo season in order.
items: The first grain is sown and a quiet time is kept.
The Twins Yam Festival is held on Friday.
Families sprinkle kpokpoi for the ancestors.
Neighbours share food on the Saturday.

activities.prompt: Sharing food with neighbours is part of Homowo. How does sharing make a community feel?

glossary.definition: A drink poured out as a prayer or offering.
Family members who lived long ago.
Planted by scattering seeds in the soil.

Two children born to the same mother at the same time.
